I don't have the evidence in hand but here is what I can remember from off the top of my head:

  • There is definitely a wage gap.

  • It is in no way as big a people say. It is likely to be around 90-95 cents on the dollar but the number is hard to pin down.

The 75c figure comes from failing to control for: experience, maternity leave, age, education, job types, hour, etc.

Also you don't want an economist, you want a statistician. This kind of data gathering is a huge part of a statisticians job but is rarely a part of an economists job.

Both sides always say they have have studies, but that's kind of why I made this thread. Hopefully someone who replies might have the studies. I really like the statisticians idea, I'm probably going to take that route next.

I grabbed some data off of wikipedia for this analysis:

The wage gap when controlled for by age, experience and occupation is ~90%. A variety of researchers have found that the amount explained by external sources is [30%-50%] so we can say the wage gap is about 93%-95%.

If I were looking for conclusive data I'd wait. I'm not a huge fan of the methodology used in the majority of studies. They have small sample sizes (I am huge advocate for large sample sizes) and often fail to account for certain factors. My conclusion (not a super scientific) is that the wage gap comes from smaller raises and is function of two things: women tend to be less aggressive when arguing for salaries and a cultural bias relating to women who are assertive. I would guess that it is more the former but I don't have enough data to say either way and that is just my intuition.

This is one of those things that get me. Wikipedia can be written by anyone. Also if we say the wage gap is about 93-95%, that's a pretty exact number for people to always be "not sure of". 5% difference would be almost unnoticeable unless you had a large same size, and lots of research into it. People have been talking about this for over 50 years, how has there not been a conclusive study done? Is the general consensus is that women make 77% than men, if you don't think about it for more than a moment, but if they do the same thing as men, they probably make the same, they just choose to have kids and take different jobs?
Men are also more likely to ask for wages, and need less time off (paternity leave isn't much in the US), so there is still a slight gap. But it's nowhere near 75%.

I haven't looked at the data but a 1% margin of error isn't actually that large and in all reality it is probably large because I ignored the margin of error from the studies. If you want an actual confidence interval it would probably be closer to [89%, 99%]. You also have to remember what 1% actually is.

This is one of the things that is very hard to pin down for many reason: It changes, researchers are commonly biased, the data is sensitive, people don't like giving out the data, it's expensive to do research, etc.

The general consensus among the people who have looked at the studies (all of the ones with proper methodology) is that there is a wage gap but it is significantly smaller than the 77% figure. Pinning down the reason is going to be very hard because both the commonly accepted cuases are rather subjective; implicit bias and less aggressive negotiations for salaries.

Here

TL;DR: There is a raw wage gap of about 20% (well lower than the popular 30% myth), which can be adjusted down to 5-7% after considering various factors. It is also likely that a large amount of the 5-7% gap can be explained by other factors that aren't easy to account for the the paper's model and/or with the data available.

That's all I've got as far as studies go.
